Performance evaluation of methanogenic digester using kitchen waste
for validation of optimized hydrolysis conditions for reduction in
ammonia accumulation
Nidhi Sahu, Ganesh Sharma, B. Chandrashekhar, Niti B. Jadeja, Atya Kapley, R.A. Pandey*,
Abhinav Sharma
CSIR-National Environmental Engineering Research Institute, Nagpur 440020, India
a r t i c l e
i n f o

17 October 2018

Available online 6 February 2019
Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Process stability
Ammonia reduction
Metagenomic analysis
Optimization
Biogas
a b s t r a c t
Ammonia accumulation above the inhibitory level is the major cause of failure of anaerobic digesters
(AD) treating kitchen waste (KW). In the present investigation a biphasic system (hydrolysis and
methanogenesis) was evaluated for validation of previously optimized hydrolysis conditions [pH 7.2e7.5,
Aeration 0.19e0.22 vvm (volume of air per unit volume of media per minute), Temperature 44 - 48 C]
for reduction in ammonia accumulation in the methanogenic digester. The pre hydrolyzed KW was fed to
methanogenic reactor with the organic loading 1.16 gVS/L - 2.97 gVS/L. Speciﬁc biogas and methane yield
were 0.589 L biogas/gVSfeed and 0.321 L methane/gVSfeed under mesophilic condition, and 0.633 L biogas/
gVSfeed and 0.329 L methane/gVSfeed under thermophilic condition, respectively. The ammonia concen-
tration in the methanogenic phase remained below 250 ppm and 550 ppm under mesophilic and ther-
mophilic conditions, respectively, validate the optimized conditions for hydrolysis of KW for reduction in
ammonia accumulation in methanogenesis phase. The Microbial diversity analysis of methanogenic
phase was carried out to monitor the shifting of microbial population under mesophilic and thermophilic
conditions. Results on these aspects have also been presented and discussed in this paper.

1. Introduction
Municipal solid waste (MSW) includes waste from households,
commercial and institutional establishments, markets and street
sweepings [1]. Safe and cost-effective management of organic
fraction of MSW (OFMSW), such as kitchen waste (KW) is a sig-
niﬁcant environmental challenge for modern society. Inadequately
managed KW disposal has the potential to affect the health and
environment [2]. KW is a readily available organic-rich waste, and
has great potential for anaerobic digestion [3]. Conversion of KW
into biogas using anaerobic digestion is one of the promising ap-
proaches for solving the OFMSW management problem, since, it
also provides clean energy in the form of methane [4].
Despite the advantages of biogas production through anaerobic
digestion of KW, accumulation of by-products viz. ammonia,
hydrogen sulﬁde and long chain fatty acids has been well known for
inhibiting the process of biomethanation. Ammonia accumulation
in the biogas digester treating substrate having low C/N ratio has
been reported as a major cause of digester failure. However, there is
a large variation in the reported inhibitory ammonia concentration
(1.7e14 g/L) which depends on the inoculum, substrate, inoculum
acclimatization and environmental conditions (pH and tempera-
ture) [5,6]. Kayhanian [7] explained the theoretical relationship
between the concentrations of free ammonia and total ammonia,

and

and
concluded that in thermophilic bioreactor system free ammonia
concentration is six times greater than mesophilic system. The
most widely accepted mechanism explaining ammonia inhibition
is that elevated ammonia level causes change of intracellular pH,
increase in maintenance energy requirement, depletion of intra-
cellular potassium, and inhibition of enzyme reactions involved in
methanogenesis [8]. Accumulation of ammonia in the digester
causes shifting in the biochemical pathways towards syntrophic
acetate oxidation from aceticlastic methanogenesis [9].
The entire process of biomethanation can be carried out either
in a monophasic system, where all the four steps are carried out in a
single digester, or in a biphasic system, in which the fermentative

(hydrolysis and acidogenesis) phase is separated from the meth-
anogenic phase. As compared to monophasic system, the biphasic
system could be controlled more easily and efﬁciently [10]. Since
ammonia is produced during the hydrolysis and acidogenesis phase
only, therefore, fermentation of KW can be optimized to control
and remove most of the ammonia from hydrolysate prior to feed in
the methanogenic phase.
In our previous study, the aerobic hydrolysis of KW was studied
and statistically optimized for simultaneous solubilization and
ammonia removal by controlling pH, temperature and aeration rate
[11]. In the present study, we have described the performance of a
methanogenic digester fed with hydrolyzed KW, which was
generated under the optimized conditions. The performance of
methanogenic phase of a biphasic semi-continuous biogas digester
(substrate fed once in a day), and changes in the microbial diversity
were monitored.
Results
were compared

methane production, ammonia concentration and metagenomic
analysis for microbial diversity during the biogas digester operation
under mesophilic and thermophilic conditions.
2. Material and method
2.1. Kitchen waste processing and hydrolysis
KW
was
collected
from
different
locations
(institutional
canteen, guest house and research scholar hostel) of CSIR-National
Environmental Engineering Research Institute, Nagpur, India. The
KW mainly consisted of cooked rice, vegetable curries, pulse soup
and chapati. The collected KW was mixed and grinded to make a
uniform slurry. The KW slurry was characterized for total solids (TS)
and volatile solids (VS) using standard protocol as described in
standard methods for examination of water and waste water [12].
Hydrolysis of KW slurry was carried out separately in a
fermenter of 3 L capacity under previously optimized conditions
[pH 7.2e7.5, temperature 43e48 C, aeration 0.19e0.22 vvm (vol-
ume of air per unit volume of media per minute)] for a retention
time of 24 h [11]. The hydrolyzed KW (hydrolysate) having

154 ± 31 mg/L TAN, 55 ± 10 mg/L FAN was fed once in a day to the
methanogenic chamber for biogas production as shown in Table 1.
2.2. Biogas digester and operation
A lab-scale digester (methanogenic chamber) of 36 L working
volume and 24 L head space volume was fabricated and used for
anaerobic digestion of pre-hydrolyzed KW. The digester consisted
of inlet for feeding the hydrolyzed slurry and an outlet for the
digested slurry. The digester was equipped with a pH and tem-
perature probe to continuously monitor the parameters during the
process. The temperature of digester was controlled by a circulating
water jacket and agitator used for uniform heat transfer. The
inoculum used for starting-up the digester was collected from a
running local mesophilic biogas plant, fed with cow dung. 36 L
inoculum having 0.078 ± 0.001 gTS/mL and 0.057 ± 0.004 gVS/mL
was ﬁlled in the digester. The KW slurry (previously hydrolyzed
under optimized conditions) was fed into digester by increasing
organic loading from 1.14 gVS/L to 1.68 gVS/L under mesophilic
condition (37 C). Next, the temperature of methanogenic phase
was gradually increased by 1 C after every 3 days up to reaching
46 C to prevent heat shock during acclimatization of inoculum for
thermophilic condition at constant OLR (1.14 gVS/L). After attaining
46 C temperature, the organic loading was gradually increased
from 1.69 gVS/L to 2.98 gVS/L as shown in Table 1.
The performance of biogas digester fed with the optimally hy-
drolyzed KW, in terms of methane yield and other important pa-
rameters (ammonia, Volatile fatty acids and alkalinity) was
evaluated under mesophilic and thermophilic conditions. Quanti-
tative analysis of biogas produced was done daily by measuring
head space pressure using a pressure gauge. After taking the
reading, head space overpressure was released, so that the starting
pressure was returned to zero. The volume of biogas generated at
STP was calculated using following equations:

The quality of biogas was checked out by monitoring the
methane content in GC-TCD (Agilent) equipped with a stainless
steel Porapak Q column (column length 6 ft and ID 2 mm). The gas
samples from the biogas digester were collected in the 1 L Tedlar
bags. 100 mL of gas sample was injected in the injector port of GC-
TCD with the help of gas-tight syringe (Hamilton, USA). The run
time of analysis was preset for 2 min with the column temperature
of 50 C. The temperature of injector, oven, and detector was 100 C,
60 C and 100 C, respectively. Hydrogen was used as the carrier
gas. The result of the analysis is based on the principle that the gas
having a thermal conductivity greater then hydrogen shows the
peak at speciﬁc retention time. The peak area (Volts) of graph
corresponded to the % concentration of methane, carbon dioxide
and nitrogen in the biogas sample.
Other indicators of process stability viz. pH, alkalinity, VFA, ratio
of VFA to alkalinity and ammonia concentration were monitored
once a week using standard protocol as described in Standard
methods for the examination of water and wastewater [12].

extraction of DNA. Total genomic DNA was extracted using the Fast

2.3.2. Metagenome sequencing
Qubit ﬂuorometery was used to determine the DNA concen-
tration and purity of samples. Illumina-compatible sequencing li-
brary preparation for DNA samples was performed using NEXTFlex
DNA Sequencing Kit (Bioo Scientiﬁc) according to manufacturer
instructions. In brief, DNA shearing was performed to generate
fragments of approximately 200bp - 400bp size using CovarisS220
system (Life Technologies, USA). The fragment size distribution was
conﬁrmed on Agilent TapeStation with D1000 DNA Kit (Agilent,
Germany). Further, the sheared DNA was puriﬁed using HighPrep
beads (Magbio Genomics, USA) followed by end repair, A-tailing,
and ligation with the Illumina multiplexing adapters (Bioo Scien-
tiﬁc, Austin) according to the protocol outlined in NEXTFlex DNA
Sequencing kit. The ligated DNA was puriﬁed using HighPrep beads
and further subjected to 10 rounds of PCR (denaturation at 98 C for
2 min, cycling at 98 C for 30 sec, 65 C for 30 sec and 72 C for 60
sec, and ﬁnal extension at 72 C for 4 min) with Illumina compatible
primers provided within the kit. The resultant PCR product (Illu-
mina-compatible sequencing library) was puriﬁed using HighPrep
beads, quantiﬁed using Qubit ﬂuorometer and fragment size dis-
tribution analysis was performed on AgilentD1000 TapeStation.
KAPAqPCR quantiﬁcation kit (KAPA Biosystems; Massachusetts)
was used to quantify the Illumina-compatible sequencing library

2.3.3. Bioinformatics analysis
Phylogenetic and functional diversity of samples were analyzed
using MG-RAST (Metagenomics Rapid Annotation using Subsystem
Technology) server by submitting the assembled reads using online
account. For the analysis default parameters which included the
maximum e-value cut-off (105), minimum percent identity cut-off
(60%), minimum alignment length cut-off (15 bps) and minimum
abundance cut-off (1) were selected for ﬁltering the data from the
data selection menu. Phylogenetic and functional analysis of data
was done using REFSeq and Subsystems database.

3. Result and discussion
3.1. Performance of biogas digester
The kitchen waste hydrolyzed under optimum conditions was
fed to the biogas digester for methanogenesis. The target of hy-
drolysis optimization was to minimize ammonia accumulation in
the biogas digester. The methanogenic digester was initially oper-
ated under mesophilic conditions (37 C) for 120 days and then
under thermophilic conditions (46 C) for 150 days.
Fig. 1a and b show the biogas yields at different organic loading
rates (OLR) during mesophilic and thermophilic operations. The
mesophilic operation was started with an organic loading rate of
1.14 gVS/L which was gradually increased up to 1.68 gVS/L. Under
this condition, average daily biogas production was 17, 27 and
42 L at organic loading rates of 1.14, 1.48 and 1.68 gVS/L, respec-
tively. The thermophilic operation was started at OLR of 1.14 gVS/L
which was gradually increased up to 2.97 gVS/L. Under this con-
dition, average daily biogas production was 37, 46, 45 and 63 L at
organic loading rates of 1.14, 1.69, 1.84 and 2.6 gVS/L, respectively,
which are higher than the mesophilic operation. The average daily
methane production was also higher in thermophilic operation, at
similar OLR as shown in Fig. 1a and b.
The methane content of the biogas also increased from 36% to
54% upon an increase in the organic loading from 1.14 to 1.68 gVS/L
for mesophilic operation. In the case of thermophilic operation, the
methane content increased from 43% to 55% upon an increase in the
organic loading from 1.14 to 2.97 gVS/L (Fig. 2).
After reaching stable performance, the Speciﬁc biogas and
methane yields were 0.589 L biogas/gVSfeed and 0.321 L methane/
gVSfeed under mesophilic condition, and 0.633 L biogas/gVSfeed and
0.329 L methane/gVSfeed under thermophilic conditions respec-
tively. The average methane content in biogas produced was 48%
and 50% under mesophilic and thermophilic conditions respec-
tively. This shows the thermophilic operation of biogas digester is
more efﬁcient for higher methane recovery at similar organic
loading rates.
Fig. 3aeb shows free ammonia concentration in the biogas
digester slurry. During mesophilic operation, the free ammonia
concentration in the digester remained below 220 mg/L during the
120 days period. During thermophilic operation, the free ammonia
concentration was higher and remained below 550 ppm during 150
days of operation. Higher free ammonia concentration in case of
thermophilic operation could be explained on the basis of a rela-
tionship provided by Zhang et al. [13]; Garcia and Angenent [14]
and Strik et al. [15], according to which the higher temperature or
the higher pH, the higher amount of free ammonia produced.
Consequently, at high temperature, it is suitable to operate
biogas digester at lowest possible pH. However in our study, both
thermophilic and methanogenic digestions were operated at
similar pH (7.25e7.5), therefore higher ammonia accumulation was
observed in the case of thermophilic operation. Nevertheless, in
both the cases of this investigation, the ammonia concentration in
the digestion slurry was much lesser than that reported earlier in
the literature. Benabdallah El Hadj et al. [16] reported that the
methane generation under mesophilic and thermophilic conditions
was reduced by 50% when ammonium ion reached concentrations
of 3,860 and 5,600 mg NH4-N/L respectively at pH 7e8.5 [17]. re-
ported that mesophilic digester had signiﬁcantly lower ammonium
ion concentration (640e800 mg/L NH4eN) than those in the ther-
mophilic digester (2880e3840 mg/L NH4eN). Kayhanian [7] also
showed that free ammonia nitrogen concentration in a thermo-
philic biogas digester can be expected to be 6 times higher than in a
mesophilic digester at the same pH. Although undesirable for
methanogenesis, the ammonia concentration found in the present
study is a good indicator of the bacterial activity since ammonia is
one of the end products of microbial hydrolysis of proteins and
higher ammonia concentration could be associated to higher pro-
tein degradation due to the faster kinetics of the biological activity.
VFA, alkalinity and their ratio have been considered as impor-
tant indicators of stability of biogas digester. The measured con-
centration of VFA and alkalinity and their ratio is showed in
Fig. 4aeb. During mesophilic operation, the VFA was found to be
highly varied and reached more than 10,000 mg/L (Fig. 4a). In case
of thermophilic operation, the VFA was found to be much lower,
between 1500 and 2000 mg/L (Fig. 4b). The alkalinity was also
N. Sahu et al. / Renewable Energy 139 (2019) 110e119
112

found to be higher during mesophilic compared to the thermo-
philic operation and there was a gradual rise in alkalinity with in-
crease in OLR. This could be due to the increasing load of sodium
hydroxide used for maintaining the pH during hydrolysis of kitchen
waste under optimized conditions. During most of the operation
period, the VFA to alkalinity ratio was below 0.3 in both the cases,
which has been reported optimum for a robust biomethanation
process [18]. Lower ammonia accumulation, low VFA/alkalinity
ratio with high methane production in the biogas digester shows
that the hydrolyzed kitchen waste was suitable for methanogenesis
and hence validates the optimized conditions of kitchen waste
hydrolysis as discussed in section 3.1.
3.2. Metagenome analysis
Inoculum sample (SM-EBD), and samples collected on 54th and
75th day of biogas digester operated under mesophilic (MP-EBD)
and thermophilic conditions (TP-EBD) were analyzed for microbial
diversity. Extracted DNA libraries were in the expected size range of
300bp e 700bp on the TapeStation. The effective sequencing insert
size is 180bp e 580bp, with combined adapter size being ~120bp.
The library was found suitable for sequencing on Illumina platform.
NGS-based metagenomic approach was applied to follow the
development of the microbial community structure in the biogas
reactors at different temperature conditions. Striking reorganiza-
tion of the mesophilic microbial community into a stable thermo-
philic community without any inoculum addition was observed in

the anaerobic digester in response to temperature elevation which
means re-organization was directed by the increasing temperature
as selection pressure [19e21]. Community analysis revealed that
the general diversity of the inoculum was higher than that of the
mesophilic and thermophilic samples [21]. Noticeable changes
were observed in the microbial diversity during the whole anaer-
obic digestion period, shown in Table 2.
Reduction of bacterial count in the thermophilic condition
showed that temperature is a selection measure of microbial
diversity. At order level majority of the genera (89.1%) were com-
mon to all 3 metagenome datasets. About 2e6 bacterial orders
were unique to or shared among 2 out of 3 samples (Fig. 5a).
Hence overall the community did not distinctly differ, but there
were remarkable changes in the abundance of the microbial
members in three samples. Similarly at genera level majority of
features were common to all 3 datasets. Sample MP-EBD contained
few unique genera, 50% of which were commonly shared with SM-
EBD sample, and 50% of which were included exclusively in MP-
EBD sample as observed in Venn analysis (Fig. 5b). The list of fea-
tures categorized unique and shared across three metagenome are
enlisted in supplementary Table x1 and y1.

of total bacteria). Similarly, in the MP-EBD and TP-EBD samples
Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes and proteobacteria were the major bacte-
rial components which were 20.2%, 33.3%, and 13.5% in MP-EBD
and 16.1%, 17.6% and 21.4% in TP-EBD samples respectively (Fig. 6).
The abundance of the phylum Proteobacteria, Firmicutes and Bac-
teriodetes in the biogas digester has been reported previously. In
MP-EBD other dominating phylum were Actinobacteria (7.7%),
Euryarchaeota (6.8%) Synergistetes (2.5%) and unclassiﬁed (derived
from bacteria, 2.1%) while in the TP-EBD other dominating phylum
were Thermotogae (15.2%), Euryarchaeota (7.8%), Actinobacteria
(2.9%), Planctomycetes (2.7%) and unclassiﬁed from bacteria (2.6% of
total bacteria). The abundance of phylum Thermotogae in TP-EBD
(15.2%) was extremely higher than the SM-EBD and MP-EBD sam-
ples (0.93% and 2.9%, respectively). The changes in abundance of
these microbial communities is subject to selection of optimum
growth temperature, for example, Actinobacteria requires low
temperature for their growth therefore, showed higher abundance
at mesophilic condition and increased temperature caused reduc-
tion of their abundance at thermophilic condition and vice-versa is
applicable for Thermotogae.
3.2.1.2. Genera abundance. Bacteroides (6.3%), Candidatus Cloa-
camonas (6.2%), Clostridium (3.3%), Geobacter (2.1%), Prevotella
(1.7%), Parabacteroides (1.6%) Syntrophus (1.4%) and Treponema
(1.3%) were the dominated genera present in the inoculums
(Fig. 7a). Candidatus Cloacamonas acidaminovorans has been re-
ported for their high abundance in several anaerobic digester
operated under mesophilic condition for anaerobic digestion of
high C : N containing substrate viz. maize silage [22,23].
At mesophilic condition, microbial abundance changed during
acclimatization of inoculum for kitchen waste. Bacteroides (10%),
Clostridium (5.5%), Parabacteroides (2.4%), Prevotella (2.35%), Can-
didatus Cloacomonas (2%), Pedobacter (1.4%) present in MP-EBD as
major genera showed the breakdown and further decomposition of
kitchen waste at mesophilic condition (Fig. 7b). The presence of
Bacteroides (7%), Clostridium (3.3%), Parabacteroides (1.7%), Pre-
votella (1.3%), Pedobacter (0.5%), Treponema (0.2%) at lower fre-
quency in TP-EBD showed that these are temperature sensitive/
tolerant microbes (Fig. 7c). In thermophilic condition, Candidatus
cloacamonas, Geobacter, Syntrophus, Anaeromyxobacter, Bacillus,
Desulfovibrio, CandidatusSolibacter were the dominated genera
involved in the breakdown and fermentation of organic molecules.
The increased abundance of these genera at thermophilic condition
showed that these microbial communities are temperature tolerant
and can grow up to 50 C.
In the thermophilic sample Bacteroides (7.4%), Methanoculleus
(6.0%), unclassiﬁed genera derived from Thermotagales family
(5.3%), Clostridium (2.8%), Kosmotoga (2.6%), Geobacter (2.1%) and
Thermotoga (1.8%) were the dominated genera overall. The abun-
dance of Candidatus Cloacamonas acidaminovorans was 6.2% in SM-
EBD which was drastically reduced in the mesophilic (2%) and
thermophilic sample (2.5%). Proteome analysis indicated that
C. acidaminovorans might gain energy from sugars in the Embden-
Meyer hof pathway and from the fermentation of amino acids, and
thereby produces hydrogen and carbon dioxide [22].
The abundance of Methanoculleus (4.3%), Kosmotoga (3.4%),
Thermotoga (2.2%) were higher in TP-EBD than the SM-EBD (0.5%,
0.1%, 0.4% respectively) and the MP-EBD (1.7%, 0.5% and 0.8%
respectively). Methanoculleus marisnigri has been reported for the
ability to utilize hydrogen, formate, ethanol and a variety of sec-
ondary alcohols such as propanol and butanol, as electron donors
for methanogenesis [24,25]. This metabolic feature of Meth-
anoculleus makes it more tolerant to changes in the environmental
conditions and therefore found in dominant in TP-EBD. The hy-
perthermophilic and anaerobic bacterium Thermotoga maritima is
capable to ferment a wide variety of carbohydrates to produce ac-
etate, CO2, and H2 through a classical Embden-Meyerhof pathway
[26]. Similarly, Kosmotoga is a hydrogen producer and can grow
over a wide temperature range (20e80 C) and 20e60 g/L NaCl
concentration [27,28]. The dominance of both hydrogen producer
Thermotogae and Kosmotaga along with hydrogentrophic metha-

This is also supported by functional diversity analysis of these
samples. As showed in the Table 3 abundance of intermediate
enzyme of aceticlastic methanogenesis pathway viz. Phosphate
acetyltransferase, N5-methyltetrahydromethanopterin: coenzyme
M methyltransferase, Methyl coenzyme M reductase etc decreased
in TP-EBD sample as compared to SM-EBD and MP-EBD while
abundance of coenzyme F420-reducing hydrogenase (essential

Competition
of

and

condition has been reported by Kotsyurbenko et al. [29]. Homo-

reported to produce acetate from H2 and CO2 and also used as an
indicator of process instability [30]. High abundance of Treponema
sp. indicated deterioration in the digester. In this study, the %
abundance of Treponema sp. is reduced drastically in TP-EBD (0.2%)
as compared to SM-EBD (1.3%). Reduction of Treponema sp. abun-
dance in TP-EBD indicated the dominance of hydrogenotrophic
methanogenesis pathway and stability of digester under thermo-
philic condition.
In this study, the methane yield of AD under thermophilic
condition is found to be higher than that of mesophilic condition,
even though the free ammonia concentration is almost two times.
The metagenomic analysis revealed that higher temperature not
only affects the dissociation constant of ammonia, but also alters
the microbial diversity of the digester, resulting in switching of
methanogenesis in the digester from aceticlastic pathway to
hydrogenotrophic pathway. Since, hydrogenotrophic methanogens
are more resistant to high ammonia concentrations [9], therefore
the digester produced more methane under thermophilic and high
ammonia concentrations.
4. Conclusion
The results obtained in this study showed that under the opti-
mized hydrolysis the average methane yield of thermophilic
anaerobic digestion is higher, although the free ammonia level is
double than that of mesophilic anaerobic digestion. In both the
conditions, ammonia concentration in the slurry was found to be
